title: Repairing a bowed tabletop with timber batten braces
subtitle: Glue and screw timber battens across the underside of a cupped or bowed tabletop to pull it flat and hold it in shape
excerpt: How to flatten a bowed or cupped tabletop by fitting timber batten braces to the underside. Covers assessing the bow, wetting and weighting the surface, gluing and screwing the battens, and allowing the assembly to set.
sourceNotes: Newey and Drage, Practical Carpentry and Joinery (referenced, not reproduced). Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (referenced, not reproduced). UK furniture restoration trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A type of warp in which a board curves across its width, concave on one face and convex on the other. Caused by uneven moisture content between the faces. The face exposed to dry air shrinks; the face exposed to moisture swells. The board curves toward the dry side.

A strip of straight, dry timber (typically 50 x 25 mm or 75 x 25 mm) fixed across the grain of a panel to resist cupping or bowing. Glued and screwed to the underside of the tabletop at regular intervals. The brace must be fixed while the panel is flat or in the corrected position; it cannot straighten a bowed panel on its own without pre-loading.

content.text: tabletop is pulled flat and held by

glued and screwed across the grain on the underside. The key is to pre-load the board into the flat position before fixing the battens. Battens glued onto a still-bowed board will hold the bow in place.

Place a straight edge across the board width at several points. Measure the gap at the centre. A bow of up to 5 mm across a 900 mm width is correctable with moisture and clamping. A bow of more than 10 mm in a thin board may be too severe; weigh the value of the piece against the difficulty of the repair.

Lay the tabletop concave face down on a flat surface. Wet the convex face (the face that is now uppermost) with a damp cloth or sponge. Lay a damp piece of hessian or cloth over the whole surface, then stack heavy weight or cramps on top to press the board flat. Leave for at least 2 hours. The added moisture causes the dry convex face to swell and the board will flatten.
Glue and fit the battens while the board is flat

With the board still clamped flat, turn it over (underside up). Cut straight, dry battens of 25 × 50 mm timber to span the full width of the board. Space them at about 300 mm intervals along the length. Apply PVA wood glue to the face of each batten and position them at 90 degrees to the grain direction of the top. Drill countersunk pilot holes through the batten and into the tabletop. Drive screws to draw the battens tight. Do not drive the screws through the top surface. Leave the cramps on for at least 4 hours while the glue sets.

Remove the cramps after the glue has set (allow at least 6 hours). Allow the board to stand for 2 days at room temperature to stabilise before refinishing. Seal the underside with a coat of varnish or primer the same day: an unsealed underside will re-absorb moisture unevenly and the cup will return.

attrs.symptom: The board re-bows after removing the clamps
attrs.cause: The glue had not fully cured when the clamps were removed, or the board was not flat when the battens were fixed.
attrs.fix: Repeat the wetting and clamping process and allow 8 to 12 hours before removing clamps. Seal both surfaces to reduce future moisture movement.

attrs.symptom: Screw heads break through the tabletop face
attrs.cause: Screws too long for the board thickness, or the pilot holes were not deep enough.
attrs.fix: Use screws that are 10 mm shorter than the combined depth of batten and tabletop. Check the depth before fitting.
